## Objective

This notebook shows every analytical step directly. The code prepares the data, checks its structure, and builds four chart types with the explicit `ggplot2` grammar.

## Load packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
```
:::


## Prepare variables deliberately

`mtcars` stores cylinders, transmission, and gears as numbers. They are categories for this analysis, so the code converts them to factors before plotting.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
required_columns <- c("mpg", "cyl", "hp", "wt", "am", "gear")
missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, names(mtcars))

if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
  stop("Missing required columns: ", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
}

cars <- mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  mutate(
    cylinders = factor(cyl, levels = c(4, 6, 8)),
    transmission = factor(
      am,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")
    ),
    gears = factor(gear)
  )

glimpse(cars)
```

The prepared dataset contains 32 vehicles and 15 variables.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
chart_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
:::


## Bar chart: compare category counts

Use bars when the question is how many observations belong to each group.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cars, aes(x = cylinders, fill = cylinders)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Cars by cylinder count",
    x = "Cylinders",
    y = "Cars"
  ) +
  chart_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/cylinder-bars-1.png){fig-alt='Bar chart showing the number of cars with four, six, and eight cylinders.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Histogram: inspect a continuous distribution

The bin width controls the level of detail and should be chosen explicitly.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cars, aes(x = hp)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 25,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#2A9D8F",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Horsepower distribution",
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "Cars"
  ) +
  chart_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/horsepower-histogram-1.png){fig-alt='Histogram of horsepower values in the mtcars dataset.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Scatter plot: examine two numeric variables

Color and shape provide redundant category encodings. The fitted line summarizes association, not causality.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(
  cars,
  aes(
    x = wt,
    y = mpg,
    color = cylinders,
    shape = transmission
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#333333"
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency falls as vehicle weight rises",
    subtitle = "Point shape identifies transmission type",
    x = "Weight (1,000 lb)",
    y = "Fuel efficiency (mpg)",
    color = "Cylinders",
    shape = "Transmission"
  ) +
  chart_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/efficiency-scatter-1.png){fig-alt='Scatter plot of vehicle weight and fuel efficiency, colored by cylinder count and shaped by transmission.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Box plot: compare distributions across groups

The box plot summarizes each distribution while jittered points preserve the small sample.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cars, aes(x = transmission, y = mpg, fill = transmission)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency by transmission",
    x = "Transmission",
    y = "Fuel efficiency (mpg)"
  ) +
  chart_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/efficiency-boxplot-1.png){fig-alt='Box plots comparing fuel efficiency for automatic and manual transmissions.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Conclusion

The visible workflow demonstrates data-type decisions, accessible scales, layered chart construction, annotations, and interpretation. See the [Spanish version](es/index.qmd).
